account: 1a. Haffner: father's monthly salary (season ticket, cheques, barber, mother, wholesale market, non-perishables, nothing for the rest of the month)
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (German full text; English wording NOT FOUND)
what_it_says: Chapter 10 (the year 1923). Introduced as how life looked in the family of a high Prussian official. On the 31st or 1st the father got his monthly salary, the family's whole living, because bank balances and savings certificates had long been worthless. He tried to buy a monthly U-Bahn pass as fast as possible; cheques were written for rent and school fees; in the afternoon the whole family went to the barber; what was left went to the mother; next day the whole family and the maid, but not the father, got up at four or five and took a taxi to the wholesale market; within an hour the monthly salary of an Oberregierungsrat was spent on non-perishable food; giant cheeses, whole hams, potatoes by the hundredweight were loaded into the taxi; they were home before school began, provisioned more or less for a month's siege; for a month there was no more money.
fragments: So gestaltete sich äußerlich das Leben in der Familie eines hohen preußischen Beamten.
Am 31. oder ersten des Monats bekam mein Vater sein Monatsgehalt, das unseren Lebensunterhalt darstellte
Bankguthaben und Sparbriefe waren längst wertlos geworden.
Wieviel das Gehalt wert war, war schwer abzuschätzen
auf jeden Fall versuchte mein Vater, eine Monatskarte für die U–Bahn so schnell wie möglich zu kaufen
Dann wurden Schecks für die Miete und das Schulgeld ausgestellt,
und am Nachmittag ging die ganze Familie zum Friseur.
Was übrig blieb, wurde meiner Mutter ausgehändigt
und am nächsten Tag stand die ganze Familie, auch das Dienstmädchen, nur nicht mein Vater,
um vier oder fünf Uhr früh auf, und fuhr mit dem Taxi zum Großmarkt.
innerhalb einer Stunde wurde das Monatsgehalt eines Oberregierungsrates für unverderbliche Speisen ausgegeben.
Riesige Käse, ganze Schinken, Kartoffeln zentnerweise wurden in das Taxi geladen.
mehr oder weniger für eine einmonatige Belagerung versorgt.
Es gab einen Monat lang kein weiteres Geld.
date_of_event: 1923 (chapter 10; no month given for the salary routine; the chapter dates the dollar: August the million, September the milliard, end of October the Billion)
source_name: Sebastian Haffner, Geschichte eines Deutschen. Die Erinnerungen 1914-1933 (DVA, Stuttgart/München 2000), full-text PDF on a private site (jimcontent.com)
note: CAUTION 1: the PDF's editorial note says a gap at pp. 54-68 was back-translated from Oliver Pretzel's English; the page reader could not confirm whether chapter 10 falls in that gap, so this German wording may be a back-translation of the English 'Defying Hitler', not Haffner's own German. CAUTION 2: I could not open the English passage itself anywhere (archive.org copy is borrow-only, Scribd shows no text, Goodreads/review pages do not quote it). Any English wording for the script must be OUR translation/paraphrase of the German above, not presented as a quotation from 'Defying Hitler'. The Tagesspiegel (17 Nov 2013) retells the same passage with slightly different German words and says the father was an Oberregierungsrat; it attaches it to its paragraph on June 1923, but Haffner's text as read gives no month. The pass is a monthly U-Bahn pass ('Monatskarte'), 'season ticket' in the brief.

account: 1b. Haffner: the young and quick got rich, the old and unworldly went under; 21-year-old bank directors
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (English quoted with page number on two blogs; German full text agrees)
what_it_says: The old and unworldly had the worst of it; many driven to begging, many to suicide. The young and quick-witted did well: overnight free, rich, independent. Mental inertia and reliance on experience were punished by starvation and death; quick reaction rewarded with sudden riches. The 21-year-old bank director appeared, and the schoolboy living off stock-market tips. After stabilisation the 21-year-old bank directors had to look for clerking jobs again.
fragments: The old and unworldly had the worst of it.
Many were driven to begging, many to suicide.
The young and quick-witted did well.
Overnight they became free, rich, and independent.
It was a situation in which mental inertia and reliance on past experience were punished by starvation and death,
but rapid appraisal of new situations and speed of reaction were rewarded with sudden, vast riches.
The twenty-one-year-old bank director appeared on the scene,
and also the high school senior who earned his living from the stock-market tips of his slightly older friends.
He wore Oscar Wilde ties, organized champagne parties, and supported his embarrassed father.
Twenty-one year-old bank directors began to look around for clerking jobs again,
DE: Den Alten und Weltfremden ging es am schlechtesten.
DE: Den Jungen, Flinken ging es gut.
DE: Der einundzwanzigjährige Bankdirektor trat auf
source_name: Haffner, Defying Hitler (trans. Oliver Pretzel), p. 56, as quoted on Daily Kos (12 Oct 2005) and chicagoboyz.net/archives/11181.html; German checked in the full-text PDF
note: Blog quotations of the published English translation, with page number 56 given by Daily Kos; consistent with the German text read separately. Second URL: https://chicagoboyz.net/archives/11181.html

account: 1c. Haffner: 'the dollar' as the daily talk; everybody a shareholder; prices doubling overnight
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT
what_it_says: The dollar's exchange rate, an everyday item on the financial pages, became the barometer everyone watched. Only those who bought shares survived financially; every minor official and worker became a shareholder and paid for daily purchases by selling shares. A pound of potatoes that cost 50,000 marks yesterday cost 100,000 today; a salary of 65,000 marks brought home on Friday no longer bought a packet of cigarettes on Tuesday.
fragments: but to an otherwise quite uninteresting, everyday item in the financial pages: the exchange rate of the dollar.
The fluctuation of the dollar was the barometer by which, with a mixture of anxiety and excitement,
The only people who were able to survive financially were those that bought stocks.
Every minor official, every employee, every shift-worker became a shareholder.
Day-to-day purchases were paid for by selling shares.
In every shop, every factory, every school, share tips were whispered in one’s ear.
Anyone who had savings in a bank or bonds saw their value disappear overnight.
A pound of potatoes which yesterday had cost fifty thousand marks now cost a hundred thousand.
The salary of sixty-five thousand marks brought home the previous Friday
was no longer sufficient to buy a packet of cigarettes on Tuesday.
DE: Schon bald nach dem Ruhrkrieg schoß der Dollar auf 20 000, hielt eine Weile an, kletterte auf 40 000
DE: Im August erreichte der Dollar die Million.
DE: Im September hatte die Million keinen praktischen Wert mehr und die Milliarde wurde die Zahlungseinheit.
DE: Ende Oktober war es die Billion.
date_of_event: 1923 (after the Ruhr occupation began in January; August, September, end of October named)
source_name: Haffner, Defying Hitler (Farrar, Straus & Giroux, 2000), p. 55, quoted by Facing History; dollar/shares sentences quoted on chicagoboyz.net/archives/11181.html; German dollar sentences from the full-text PDF
note: German 'Billion' = 10^12 (a US trillion); 'Milliarde' = 10^9. Haffner's dollar steps are a memoirist's round figures, not a rate table.

account: 2. Stefan Zweig, The World of Yesterday: the German inflation
verdict: ORIGINAL (published English translation, full text on archive.org; British edition)
what_it_says: After Rathenau's murder (he was at Westerland that day) the mark plunged; the Austrian inflation at 15,000 to 1 was child's play beside it. He paid 50,000 marks for a newspaper in the morning and 100,000 in the evening. He sent his publisher a manuscript he had worked on for a year and asked for an advance on 10,000 copies; by the time the cheque was deposited it hardly paid the postage of a week before. Tram fares in millions, lorries carrying paper money from the Reichsbank, 100,000-mark notes in the gutter thrown away by a beggar. Shoelaces cost more than a shoe, then more than a fashionable shoe shop with 2,000 pairs; a broken window more than the house; a book more than the printing works with a hundred presses. For 20 pounds (US edition: a hundred dollars) rows of six-storey houses on the Kurfürstendamm; factories for the old price of a wheelbarrow. Boys who found a forgotten case of soap in the harbour lived like kings for months selling a cake a day. Stinnes the super-profiteer. The unemployed shook their fists at profiteers and foreigners in cars. Each billion (10^12) of inflated marks was exchanged for one new mark. Nothing embittered the Germans so much or made them so ripe for Hitler.
fragments: On that day, I was already in Westerland.
our Austrian inflation with its absurd enough ratio of 15,000 old to 1 of new currency had been shabby child's-play.
I have known days when I had to pay fifty thousand marks for a newspaper in the morning and a hundred thousand in the evening
For instance, I sent a manuscript to my publisher on which I had worked for a year;
to be on the safe side I asked for an advance payment of royalties on ten thousand copies.
By the time the cheque was deposited, it hardly paid the postage I had put on the parcel a week before;
on street-cars one paid in millions, lorries carried the paper money from the Reichsbank to the other banks,
and a fortnight later one found hundred-thousand-mark notes in the gutter; a beggar had thrown them away contemptuously.
A pair of shoe laces cost more than a shoe had once cost, no, more than a fashionable store
with two thousand pairs of shoes had cost before.
to repair a broken window more than the whole house had formerly cost, a book more than the printer's works with a hundred presses.
For £20 one could buy rows of six-storey houses on Kurfürstendamm, and factories were to be had for the old
US edition: For a hundred dollars one could buy rows of six-story houses on the Kurfürstendamm,
US edition: and factories were to be had for the old equivalent of a wheelbarrow.
Some adolescent boys who had found a case of soap forgotten in the harbour disported themselves for months in cars
and lived like kings, selling a cake every day, while their parents, formerly well-to-do, slunk about like beggars.
Towering over all of them was the gigantic figure of the super-profiteer Stinnes.
The unemployed stood around by the thousands and shook their fists at the profiteers and foreigners in their luxurious cars.
each billion of artificially inflated marks was exchanged for a single new mark, a norm had been created.
Nothing ever embittered the German people so much — it is important to remember this —
nothing made them so furious with hate and so ripe for Hitler as the inflation.
date_of_event: from 24 June 1922 (Rathenau's murder) to the stabilisation; Zweig gives no dates for the single scenes
source_name: Stefan Zweig, The World of Yesterday (English translation, Indian digitisation of the British edition; pp. 237-240 of that printing), archive.org full text; US-edition wording from alphahistory.com/weimarrepublic/stefan-zweig-1923-hyperinflation-1943/
read_how: page text (OCR; I corrected obvious OCR slips: 'milhons', 'bilhon', 'Kurfiirstendamm', '^20', 'I' for 1)
note: Two published English wordings exist: the British printing says 'For £20', the US (Viking 1943) printing says 'For a hundred dollars'. Do not treat either figure as a measured price: it is Zweig's rhetoric, written about 1941. Zweig lived in Salzburg and visited Germany; this is a memoir written two decades later, not a Berlin diary. The stabilisation sentence in the book places it loosely; the page reader's summary said '1924', which the book may say, but the Rentenmark dates from 15 Nov 1923. Translator not visible on the pages read.

account: 3a. Hemingway, 'Crossing to Germany Is Way to Make Money' (Kehl), Toronto Daily Star, 19 Sept 1922
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (full article text reproduced by German History in Documents and Images)
what_it_says: From Strasbourg by tram to Kehl. For 10 francs (about 90 Canadian cents) he got 670 marks; after a day's spending he and his wife had 120 marks left. Five apples cost 12 marks (under 2 cents); an old man with a white beard asked the price and could not afford it. Peas 18 marks a pound, beans 16; beer 10 marks a stein; a five-course hotel meal 120 marks (15 cents); the French cross the bridge and eat cream cakes at 5 marks a slice; a pastry shop is swept clean in half an hour.
fragments: For ten francs I received 670 marks.
Ten francs amounted to about ninety cents in Canadian money.
we had one hundred and twenty marks left!
We picked out five very good-looking apples and gave the old woman a fifty-mark note.
She gave us back thirty-eight marks in change.
I counted the change and told him twelve marks.
Twelve marks, on that day, amounted to a little under two cents.
With marks at 800 to the dollar, or 8 to a cent
Peas were 18 marks a pound, beans 16 marks a pound
Beer was 10 marks a stein, or 1-1/4 cents.
served a five-course table d’hôte meal for 120 marks, which amounts to 15 cents in our money
The same meal could not be duplicated in Strasbourg, three miles away, for a dollar.
gorged on fluffy, cream-filled slices of German cake at five marks the slice
The contents of a pastry shop are swept clean in half an hour.
source_name: German History in Documents and Images (GHI Washington), 'Ernest Hemingway: Inflation Stories (1922)', citing the Archive of American Journalism
note: The same page has 'Germans are Doggedly Sullen or Desperate Over the Mark' (Freiburg, 1 Sept 1922): 'Four of us stayed four days in a Freiburg hotel and the bill amounted to 2,200 marks, or about 20 cents a day apiece.' and a line that the mark 'has dropped to 22,000 to the dollar' beside 'at 800 to the dollar' (the figures in that article look inconsistent on the page; use only the Kehl article's 800). Fergusson's retelling gives the hotel meal as 150 marks; GHDI's text says 120. This is 1922, and Kehl, not Berlin 1923.

account: 4. Pearl S. Buck / Erna von Pustau, How It Happens (1947)
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (quoted by Fergusson with Buck's permission; the book itself is not online)
what_it_says: Erna von Pustau (Fergusson: her 'father was a small Hamburg businessman who ran a fishmarket'; interviewed by Pearl Buck 'many years afterwards'), as quoted in Fergusson: people said 'the dollar is going up again' when really the mark was falling; at the end of 1922 two rolls cost 20 marks in the morning and 25 in the afternoon; her mother sold rented houses for twice what was paid and found furniture had risen fivefold; in the Ruhr struggle even her father gave money and they sat in cold houses; in summer 1923 mail carriers pushed sacks and prams of paper money that would be devalued next day; 'the Middle Ages came back'; her father turned to blaming 'Jewish capital'.
fragments: whose father was a small Hamburg businessman who ran a fishmarket
We used to say 'The dollar is going up again', while in reality the dollar remained stable but our mark was falling.
'By the end of the year,' said Erna von Pustau,
'my allowance and all the money I earned were not worth one cup of coffee.
You could go to the baker in the morning and buy two rolls for 20 marks; but go there in the afternoon and the same two rolls were 25 marks.
The baker didn't know how it happened … His customers didn't know …
It had somehow to do with the dollar, somehow to do with the stock exchange — and somehow, maybe, to do with the Jews.'
They replied candidly that they were paying off their mortgages.
Inflation finished the process of moral decay which the war had started
we of the middle class are not organised against the wholesalers, while the workers are organised against us.
All the old patriotic songs were sung
Even Father gave money to help the Ruhr.
We had cold houses again, but we were willing to suffer cold for our fatherland.
The Middle Ages came back,
You could see mail carriers in the streets with sacks on their backs or pushing baby carriages
before them, loaded with paper money that would be devalued the next day,
Life was madness, nightmare, desperation, chaos.
You should have known my father as he used to be,
The winners in our inflation were big-business men in the cities...the great losers were the working class
and above all the middle class, who had the most to lose.
date_of_event: end of 1922 (the rolls); early 1923 (Ruhr); summer/August 1923 (mail carriers, per Fergusson's placement)
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, chs. 1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 (he states extracts from How It Happens are reprinted with permission); last two fragments from rudy.substack.com/p/a-very-ordinary-life quoting the book
read_how: page text of Fergusson / of the Substack post
note: NOT FOUND in anything I could open: 'prices doubling between getting paid and reaching the shop', a 'pound of cheese', or a 'printing presses' passage in her words. The rolls (20 to 25 marks, morning to afternoon, end of 1922) is the nearest thing. She was in Hamburg, not Berlin, and spoke to Buck about 1945-47. The PBS/'Paper Money' essay quotes Pearl Buck ('They had lost their fortunes, their savings; they were dazed and inflation-shocked and did not understand') and calls it Buck writing about a 1923 visit to Germany: unverified attribution, treat with caution. No archive.org full text of How It Happens was found. The rolls sentence came back whole from the reader (longer than its usual cap): re-check before quoting. 'By the end of the year' = end of 1922 by Fergusson's placement in ch. 8.

verdict: RETELLING ONLY (quoted in Fergusson; An Ambassador of Peace itself did not turn up as full text)
what_it_says: As quoted by Fergusson: Aug 1922 a card shows the dollar at 1,837, 'an enormous fall since yesterday'; stopping the press 'requires handcuffs'; Dec 1922 'the tail goes faster than the dog'; on Havenstein's 17 Aug 1923 speech he noted the sums in pounds and that no one on the Council criticised the policy 'or referred to its insanity'; mid-August 1923 a golf green fee of a million marks is about a shilling for a foreigner while the housewife queues for hours for butter; 21 Oct 1923 at 60 milliards to the pound, about one mark for every second since the birth of Christ; Oct 1923 a beggar would hardly accept a smaller note; Christmas Day 1923, queues have disappeared.
fragments: an enormous fall since yesterday
it requires handcuffs
The tail goes faster than the dog.
It is fatal in the end, but it gets its votaries over many difficult moments.
Forty-six billion marks [12 noughts] represent a face value of £2,300,000,000,000
The Council of State is supposed to contain financial and economic experts,
yet none criticised the policy stated or referred to its insanity.
The Reichsbank's own demented inspirations give stabilisation no chance.
It is vexatious enough for a foreigner to be asked for a green fee at the golf course of one million marks, but he can console himself that in his case it amounts to about a shilling.
has to stand in a queue for several hours to get some articles like butter.
approximately equal to one mark for every second which has elapsed since the birth of Christ.
a beggar would hardly accept any smaller note.
Animals crowd the abattoirs and queues have disappeared from before the shops of butchers and provision merchants.
Not even the most fanatical advocate of stabilization ,
could have anticipated more remarkable results .
date_of_event: 24 Aug 1922; Dec 1922; after 17 Aug 1923; mid-Aug 1923; 21 Oct 1923; 25 Dec 1923
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, chs. 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 (D'Abernon's diary and Foreign Office despatches); the Christmas 1923 'fanatical advocate' fragments from Financial History 142 (Summer 2022), p. 35
read_how: page text of Fergusson; the golf-fee sentence came back whole from the reader and exceeds its usual length, so re-check before quoting it
note: Fergusson mixes D'Abernon's printed diary with unpublished despatches and does not always say which. 'Billion' here is the British 10^12. Bodleian lists his 1923 diary manuscripts but no text online.

account: 6. Havenstein's statement of 17 August 1923 on the note-printing effort
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (Fergusson quoting the speech in English; no German original opened)
what_it_says: Speaking to a 'Council of State' on 17 August 1923, in a speech published at once, Havenstein said the Reichsbank was issuing 20,000 milliard (20 trillion) marks of new money daily, 5,000 milliards of it in large denominations; next week 46,000 milliards daily, 18,000 in large denominations; the total issue stood at 63,000 milliards; so in a few days it could issue in one day two-thirds of the total circulation. Later in August he told the Reichsbank central committee the sums were barely adequate and that some banks could be supplied only by aeroplane.
fragments: The full enormity of Havenstein's policies was duly revealed in the speech he made
published immediately afterwards — to a Council of State on August 17.
'The Reichsbank,' he said, with evident pride and satisfaction,
'today issues 20,000 milliard marks of new money daily, of which 5,000 milliards are in large denominations.
In the next week the bank will have increased this to 46,000 milliards daily,
of which 18,000 milliards will be in large denominations.
The total issue at present amounts to 63,000 milliards.
In a few days we shall therefore be able to issue in one day two-thirds of the total circulation.'
These enormous sums are barely adequate to cover the vastly increased demand for the means of payment.
The deliveries to several banks can be made … only by aeroplanes.
source_name: Adam Fergusson, When Money Dies (1975), ch. 11 'Havenstein'
note: 'with evident pride and satisfaction' is Fergusson's gloss, not a record. Which body the 'Council of State' was (Reichsrat? Reichswirtschaftsrat?) is not settled by Fergusson; say 'a government council'. Two New Zealand papers of 20-21 Aug 1923 ('RECORD IN MARKS') appear to carry the cabled report but Papers Past returned only a bot-check page. Kurt Singer's 'Der Fall Havenstein' (Wirtschaftsdienst 1923, Heft 33) opened but does not quote the speech; it does record the street name 'Havensteinrubel' for the August 1923 million notes.

account: 7a. Contemporary newspaper: Friedrich Kroner, 'Überreizte Nerven' / 'Overwrought Nerves', Berliner Illustrirte Zeitung, 26 Aug 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (English translation from The Weimar Republic Sourcebook, reproduced by GHDI)
what_it_says: Berlin, late August 1923. Queues, mostly women in kitchen dresses, form again outside shops; the city will be 'shopped empty'. Rice was 80,000 marks a pound yesterday and 160,000 today. A sign offers 'cheaper butter' at 1,400,000 instead of 1,600,000 marks. The brand-new note paid out as a weekly wage, still moist from the printers, shrinks in value on the way to the grocer. A quarrel at a dairy counter ends with police and charges.
fragments: There is not much to add.
It pounds daily on the nerves: the insanity of numbers, the uncertain future
lines of shoppers, long since an unaccustomed sight, once more form in front of shops
The lines always send the same signal: the city, the big stone city will be shopped empty again.
Rice, 80,000 marks a pound yesterday, costs 160,000 marks today, and tomorrow perhaps twice as much
“Cheaper butter! Instead of 1,600,000 marks, just 1,400,000 marks.”
The piece of paper, the spanking brand-new bank note, still moist from the printers
shrinks in value on the way to the grocer's shop.
Barley, groats, beans, lentils—always the same, buy, buy, buy.
their hastily donned kitchen dresses, their careworn, patient faces.
They rise with the dollar, hate, desperation, and need—daily emotions like daily rates of exchange.
“Two dozen turnips.” “There’s only one dozen.”
And charges are filed.
source_name: German History in Documents and Images, from Kaes/Jay/Dimendberg (eds.), The Weimar Republic Sourcebook (University of California Press, 1994), pp. 63-64
note: The best Berlin shopping scene found. The butter price has no weight unit in the fragment read (probably per pound: do not state the unit). The Smithsonian article's late-1923 prices (meat 3 billion a pound etc.) were not in the Kroner text as read.

account: 7b. Contemporary newspaper: Hamburger Echo, 15 November 1923 (the day the Rentenmark was issued)
verdict: ORIGINAL (digitised newspaper, OCR of Fraktur: imperfect)
what_it_says: Hamburg, Thursday 15 Nov 1923. The Rentenbank has begun issuing its notes. One gold mark = 300 milliard marks. Half a loaf costs 73 milliard marks (bread and sugar cards still to be kept). Postage: local letter 5 milliard, postcard 2 milliard, long-distance letter 10 milliard. Tram and elevated railway fares already in gold pfennigs (10, 15, 20). Readers who have not yet paid this week's subscription pay 400 milliard marks from today. Dollar unit rate of 14 Nov about 1.26 billion (10^12) marks; Berlin official rate about 2.5 billion.
fragments: Der Preis für ein halbes Brot beträgt 73 Milliarden Mark.
Stadtbrief 5 Milliarden, Postkarte 2 Milliarden, Fernbrief 10 Milliarden, Fern-Postkarte 5 Milliarden.
Hoch- und Straßenbahn: Wochentags 10, 15, 20 Goldpfennige
Die Deutsche Rentenbank hat, entsprechend der ihr erteilten Ermächtigung, mit der Ausgabe der Rentenbankscheine begonnen
Eine Goldmark — 300 Milliarden Mark.
zahlen von heute ab 400 Milliarden Mark.
source_name: Hamburger Echo, Nr. 316, 15 Nov 1923, Staats- und Universitätsbibliothek Hamburg (digitised)
read_how: page text (OCR; I normalised obvious OCR letters such as 'ber' for 'der', 'Postkatte')

account: 7d. Morgan Philips Price, Daily Herald Berlin correspondent, dispatch of 18 October 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (GHDI, from his collected dispatches)
what_it_says: The mark has ceased to be a currency and is just packets of paper standing for dollars or pounds; the number of packets per dollar changes daily; a thing costs so much at ten in the morning and so much at five in the afternoon; those with foreign currency get along.
fragments: It cost me at ten o'clock this morning so much, and at five o'clock this afternoon so much
The mark has ceased to be currency and is merely a vast mass of paper packets representing so many dollars or pounds.
The number of packets to the dollar varies every day
Those who are lucky enough to have foreign currency can get along, but even then with difficulty.
source_name: GHDI, from M. Philips Price, Dispatches from the Weimar Republic (Pluto Press, 1999), pp. 169-70
note: No prices in it.

account: 8a. Betty Scholem to Gershom Scholem, Berlin, 15 and 23 October 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (published English translation of the letters, reproduced by GHDI)
what_it_says: 15 Oct: this letter cost 15 million to post, 30 million from the day after tomorrow. The family printing firm bought dollars on Friday at 1.5 billion to keep next week's payroll, to re-sell on Thursday; this week's pay 8 billion, workers demand double. Bread card abolished; a normal loaf 540 million, tomorrow surely double. Tram fare 20 million, tomorrow 50. A bank cheque for over 5 million cost 40 million in fees. A rabbit eaten for 1.75 billion. 23 Oct: 'lucky we're in the business of printing money'; 130 workers again; the sons busy day and night with money transactions, more bankers than publishers; in three days the dollar went 10, 18.5, 40 billion; bread 900 million, 2.5 billion, 5.5 billion; some plundering.
fragments: Notice that this letter cost 15 million cash; it will be 30 million beginning the day after tomorrow
Now you can get things done only with billions.
To ensure that next week’s payroll will keep its value, the boys bought dollars on Friday
at the (ridiculous!!) exchange rate of 1.5 billion to 1
For the time being, this week’s pay will be 8 billion,
The bread ration card has been done away with, and a normal loaf of bread now costs 540 million;
tomorrow, surely twice as much.
The streetcar fare is 20 million (tomorrow it’ll be 50!).
My God, you probably don’t have faintest notion of this million-fold witches’ Sabbath.
When we went to the bank here in Berlin to pick it up, it cost 40 million in transfer fees!
They ate a rabbit for 1.75 billion.
It’s lucky we’re in the business of printing money.
Once again, we have 130 workers.
They are now more bankers than book publishers.
In three days the dollar has gone from 10 billion, to 18.5 billion, to 40.
Bread: 900 million, 2.5 billion, 5.5 billion.
Here and there plundering has flared up, but not much.
source_name: GHDI, from Gershom Scholem, A Life in Letters, 1914-1982, ed./trans. Anthony David Skinner (Harvard UP, 2002), pp. 125-27; German: Mutter und Sohn im Briefwechsel 1917-1946 (C.H. Beck, 1989), pp. 84-89
note: The strongest dated Berlin household source found: letter postage, bread, tram, payroll, all with dates. 'Billion' in this American translation = 10^9 (German Milliarde). No Rentenmark letter was on the page.

account: 8b. Victor Klemperer, diary, 2/3 August 1923: the price that doubled while the coffee was drunk
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (quoted with edition and page by Volker Ullrich; also in the Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek exhibition)
what_it_says: On the way back from a Baltic holiday, Klemperer's wife Eva ordered a cup of coffee in a station waiting room. The price board said 6,000 marks; it vanished while she drank; the waiter asked 12,000. She said it had said 6,000. 'Oh, you were here during the old price? Then pay 6,000!'
fragments: Die Preistafel zeigte 6000 M. Das verschwand, während sie trank.
Beim Kassieren verlangte der Kellner 12000.
Sie sagte, es hätte doch vorhin dort 6000 gestanden.
Ach, Sie waren schon während des alten Preises hier?
Dann zahlen Sie 6000!
Auf der Rückfahrt von ihrem Urlaub an der Ostsee bestellte seine Frau Eva in einem Wartesaal eine Tasse Kaffee:
date_of_event: diary entry of 2/3 August 1923 (Klemperer lived in Dresden; the waiting room's town is not given)
source_name: Volker Ullrich in Aus Politik und Zeitgeschichte 4/2023, pp. 10-16, fn. 9: Klemperer, Leben sammeln, nicht fragen wozu und warum. Tagebücher 1918-1924, ed. Walter Nowojski (Berlin 1996), p. 725; same quotation at https://ausstellungen.deutsche-digitale-bibliothek.de/en/krisenjahr-1923
note: This is the one dated, first-hand original behind the 'coffee cost more by the time you drank it' story, and in it the waiter lets her pay the OLD price. The last fragment is Ullrich's lead-in, not Klemperer's words. Other Klemperer lines ('Germany is collapsing in an eerie, step-by-step manner', 'How long will we still have something to eat?', '150 paper millions are 0.015 pfennigs') were seen only undated in Smithsonian / Facing History (the latter citing Evans, The Coming of the Third Reich, p. 107): RETELLING ONLY.

account: 8c. Käthe Kollwitz, diary, October-November 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (GHDI translation from Die Tagebücher, 1989, pp. 543-44, 561-63)
what_it_says: 22 Oct 1923: the dollar at 40 billion, a general strike announced, hunger and confusion everywhere. November: a child on the tram sees the telegraph wires and asks 'Mother, is that the dollar?'; her grandson asks his mother how the dollar is doing. End of November: a loaf costs 140 billion (later 80 billion); relatives lose their jobs; the unemployed swarm the streets.
fragments: the dollar stands at 40 billion, a general strike has been announced for tomorrow, hunger and confusion everywhere.
Mother, is that the dollar?
How is the dollar doing?
Hunger! One loaf of bread costs 140 billion!
Hunger, hunger everywhere.
The unemployed swarm the streets.
source_name: GHDI, 'Käthe Kollwitz on Hyperinflation (1922/1923)'
note: 'Billion' here = 10^9 (Milliarde). The fall to 80 billion came from the reader's paraphrase, not a quoted string.

account: 8d. Harry Graf Kessler, diary, 7 Nov 1922 and 4 Dec 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (quoted with volume and page by Volker Ullrich)
what_it_says: 7 Nov 1922: the dollar rate shows the progress of our decline daily, like a gravely ill man's fever chart (dollar then about 9,000 marks). 4 Dec 1923, Berlin: one sees cheerful women shoppers in the food shops again; a first ray of hope.
fragments: Wie die Fieberkurve eines Schwerkranken zeigt der Dollarstand täglich den Fortschritt unseres Verfalls
Man sieht in den Lebensmittelgeschäften wieder vergnügte Käuferinnen.
Ein erster Hoffnungsstrahl dringt durch das Dunkel
source_name: Ullrich, APuZ 4/2023, fn. 7 and 30: Kessler, Das Tagebuch 1880-1937, vol. 7 (Stuttgart 2007), p. 567; vol. 8 (2009), p. 167
note: Thea Sternheim: NOT FOUND (nothing opened).

account: 8e. 'Wolfgang', a Berliner, letters to the American composer Edgar Stillman Kelley, 2 and 17 February 1923
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (GHDI translation of archival letters)
what_it_says: Early in the Ruhr crisis: a litre of milk 560 marks; an egg 2 US cents; an iron two-litre cooking pot 30,000 marks ($1.60) yesterday; shoes 60,000 to 120,000 marks; every purchase a senseless luxury; in his house, where many old ladies live on small pensions, someone dies of exhaustion almost every week.
fragments: A liter of milk now costs 560 marks.
1 egg = 2 cents !!!
A simple iron 2-liter cooking pot still cost 30,000 marks or 1.60 dollars yesterday
Here, shoes still cost between 60,000 and 120,000 marks or 3½ to 6½ dollars
every purchase becomes a senseless luxury
Berlin has gone completely insane!
In our house, where many old ladies live on small pensions, almost every week someone dies of exhaustion
source_name: GHDI, 'Letters to America Reflect the Effects of Hyperinflation in Berlin (February 1923)'; Edgar Stillman Kelley Collection, Western College Memorial Archives, Oxford, Ohio, Box 17
note: The reader did not say which of the two dates each price belongs to.

account: 9a. Fergusson anecdote: baskets/suitcases stolen and the money left; coffee 5,000 to 8,000 marks
verdict: ORIGINAL for Fergusson's wording; UNSOURCED there
what_it_says: Fergusson (ch. 9, pp. 83-84) introduces these as 'There were stories': thieves stole the baskets and suitcases in which shoppers carried money and left the money on the ground; restaurant meals cost more when the bill came than when ordered; a 5,000-mark cup of coffee cost 8,000 by the time it was drunk. He names no witness or document. It is baskets and suitcases, not 'two women with a laundry basket'.
fragments: There were stories of shoppers who found that thieves had stolen the baskets and suitcases in which they carried their money
leaving the money itself behind on the ground
There were stories (many of them, as the summer wore on and as exchange rates altered several times a day)
of restaurant meals which cost more when the bills came than when they were ordered.
A 5,000-mark cup of coffee would cost 8,000 marks by the time it was drunk.
queueing impatiently outside the pay windows with big shopping bags in which to rush their wages away to the shops
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, ch. 9
note: In the script these must be worded as stories people told ('the story went'), not as events. For the coffee, use Klemperer's dated diary entry (8b) instead. A second version (Goodman/'Adam Smith', Paper Money, 1981, on PBS): a Freiburg student, menu price 5,000, two cups, bill 14,000, told to order both at once; unnamed, unsourced.

account: 9b. Life savings / insurance policy bought one loaf (or a stamp, a cup of coffee)
verdict: RETELLING ONLY
what_it_says: Goodman quotes the oil consultant Walter Levy: his father, a lawyer, took out a 20-year insurance policy in 1903, paid every month, and when it came due cashed it in and bought a single loaf of bread. Erna von Pustau (in Fergusson): by the end of 1922 her allowance and earnings were 'not worth one cup of coffee'. No sourced version with a postage stamp was found.
fragments: "My father was a lawyer," says Walter Levy.
and he had taken out an insurance policy in 1903, and every month he had made the payments faithfully.
It was a 20-year policy, and when it came due, he cashed it in and bought a single loaf of bread.
source_name: George J. W. Goodman ('Adam Smith'), Paper Money (1981), pp. 57-62, excerpt on PBS Commanding Heights
note: A son's recollection told to a journalist about 1980: attributable ('one man recalled'), not checkable.

account: 9c. Workers paid at 11 am, a siren, a lorry of notes, a dash to the shops
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Goodman's Paper Money; original source not traced)
what_it_says: Goodman gives it as an unnamed factory worker's description of payday: at 11 a siren sounded, everyone gathered in the forecourt where a five-ton lorry stood brimful of paper money; the chief cashier and assistants climbed on top, read out names and threw bundles of notes.
fragments: At 11:00 in the morning a siren sounded, and everybody gathered in the factory forecourt,
where a five-ton lorry was drawn up loaded brimful with paper money.
The chief cashier and his assistants climbed up on top.
They read out names and just threw out bundles of notes.
source_name: Goodman, Paper Money (1981), on PBS; also inflationdata.com citing the same book
note: Not in Fergusson. Goodman does not name the worker. From memory only, NOT read in this session: the passage is usually credited to William Guttmann and Patricia Meehan, The Great Inflation (1975), with a named witness; that book did not open and this attribution is unverified. Fergusson's nearest sourced equivalents: Curt Riess (wages paid weekly, then every three days, then daily; workers 'rushed to the nearby shops', GHDI) and Dorothea Günther (father paid daily, see 'other details').

account: 9d. The two brothers (one saved, one drank and sold the empty bottles)
verdict: NOT FOUND
what_it_says: No source of any kind was found in this session; it is not in the parts of Fergusson read (all chapters were queried).
note: Treat as folklore. Do not use as fact.

account: 10. Photographs with archive captions
verdict: ORIGINAL captions for six archive photos; children/stove photos NOT VERIFIED
what_it_says: (a) Wallpapering with banknotes: Bundesarchiv, Aktuelle-Bilder-Centrale, Georg Pahl, Bild 102-00104, dated 1923 by GHDI. (b) Queue outside a Berlin food shop: bpk 30014556 = Bundesarchiv Bild 146-1971-109-42, 1923; the Bundesarchiv title names the shop as the butter shop of Gebrüder Groh. (c) Money transport for a small firm's payroll, Halle (Saale), 1923: DHM Inv. F 75/589. (d) 'Geldtransport mit Reisekörben' (money carried in travelling baskets), 1923: Bundesarchiv BildY 1-390-10206. (e) 'Berlin, Geldtransport mit Taschen', July 1923: Bundesarchiv Bild 102-00133. (f) 'Verkauf und Reparaturen im Tausch gegen Lebensmittel', 1923: DHM Inv. F 85/526; the DHM page does not give the sign's wording or the kind of shop. (g) Reichsbank destroying banknotes: Bundesarchiv Bild 102-00238 is dated January 1924 by the DDB exhibition (after stabilisation), and a similar one, Bild 102-11825 'Banknoten werden vernichtet!', is dated June 1931. (h) Children with stacks of notes, the kite, the woman feeding a stove: found only on agency and aggregator pages; Getty's children-with-a-stack photo carries a placeholder creation date of 1 January 1919 and the credit Universal History Archive; rarehistoricalphotos gives '1923' and '1922' with no archive credit. No archive record was found that dates them.
fragments: Wallpapering with worthless banknotes, 1923.
Geldtransport für die Lohnauszahlung eines kleinen Betriebes während der Inflation
Geldtransport mit Reisekörben
Berlin, Geldtransport mit Taschen
Verkauf und Reparaturen im Tausch gegen Lebensmittel
Inflation, Schlange vor Lebensmittelgeschäft, Berlin
Deutsche Reichsbank, Vernichtung von Banknoten
Banknoten werden vernichtet!
Im August 1923 kostete in Deutschland ein Kilo Brot aufgrund der Inflation rund 69.000 Mark
Children stand next to a tower of 100,000 marks, equal in value to one US dollar. 1923.
A woman uses banknotes to light her stove. 1923.
date_of_event: 1923 (a-f); January 1924 and June 1931 (g); undated in any archive (h)
source_name: Deutsche Digitale Bibliothek virtual exhibition 'Das Krisenjahr 1923' (with Bundesarchiv and DHM); GHDI image pages; dhm.de/lemo/bestand/objekt/verkauf-im-tausch-gegen-lebensmittel-1923.html; osmand mirror of Wikimedia Commons for Bild 102-11825; gettyimages.dk 464784941; rarehistoricalphotos.com
read_how: page text (captions as listed by the reader; I did not see the images)
note: For the script and thumbnail: do not caption the children-with-banknote-blocks, kite or stove scenes '1923' as fact. Many such pictures are thought to date from after stabilisation, when the notes were waste paper, but I found no archive statement either way in this session: say 'when the notes were worthless'. The last two fragments are aggregator captions, not archive captions. DHM also says bread was 'über 200 Milliarden Mark' a kilo in November 1923 (reader's paraphrase).

account: 11. First-hand accounts of the Rentenmark's arrival and the weeks after
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (several)
what_it_says: Nothing changed overnight. Kessler, Berlin, 4 Dec 1923: cheerful women shoppers in the food shops again, a first ray of hope. D'Abernon, 25 Dec 1923: queues have disappeared from butchers and provision shops. D'Abernon, 31 Dec 1923: the crisis year ends; only looking back does one see how near the abyss the country stood. Haffner: small ugly grey-green notes, wages suddenly paid in Rentenmark, the dollar and shares stopped rising. Kuczynski to the British ambassador, Feb 1924: the change in public feeling is astounding and mainly psychological. Frau Barten of East Prussia (Goodman): the feeling of having one Rentenmark; she bought a small tin bread bin. Historians: Ullrich says the 'miracle of the Rentenmark' did not come overnight; Fergusson says three days after stabilisation no more food had reached the markets and it appeared in towns about mid-December.
fragments: Es dauerte einige Zeit, bis das Publikum Zutrauen zum neuen Zahlungsmittel fasste.
Doch Anfang Dezember waren die Zeichen der Besserung bereits zu erkennen.
Man sieht in den Lebensmittelgeschäften wieder vergnügte Käuferinnen.
Das „Wunder der Rentenmark“ trat nicht über Nacht ein.
Am 14. November überstieg der Dollarkurs erstmals die Billionengrenze, am 15. stand er bei 2,52 Billionen.
An diesem Tag wurde eine neue Währung, die Rentenmark, ausgegeben.
Am 20. November konnte der Kurs des Dollars bei 4,2 Billionen stabilisiert werden.
Animals crowd the abattoirs and queues have disappeared from before the shops of butchers and provision merchants.
Nun geht das Krisenjahr zu Ende
wie nah dieses Land am Abgrund stand
The difference in public feeling compared with two months ago is absolutely astounding.
"I remember," said one Frau Barten of East Prussia, "the feeling of having just one Rentenmark to spend."
I bought a small tin bread bin.
Just to buy something that had a price tag for one Mark was so exciting.
Hitler's greatest enemy is the Rentenmark.
No one imagines the Renten-mark will help.
date_of_event: 15 Nov 1923 (issue); 20 Nov (rate fixed at 4.2 Billionen); 4 Dec, 25 Dec, 31 Dec 1923; Feb 1924
source_name: Ullrich, APuZ 4/2023 (Kessler vol. 8 p. 167; D'Abernon, Ein Botschafter der Zeitwende II, pp. 337f.); Fergusson chs. 12-13 (D'Abernon, Clive, Kuczynski); Goodman on PBS (Frau Barten); Haffner ch. 10
note: No diary entry dated 15 November 1923 itself was found. The last two fragments are the British consul-general in Munich, Robert Clive (October 1923 doubt; end of 1923 verdict), from Fergusson. The 'shops suddenly full next morning' picture is not supported by any source read; the sources say weeks.

account: 12. People who won
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Fergusson reporting two witnesses) plus one sourced general statement
what_it_says: (a) Hans-Georg von der Osten, a former pilot of Richthofen's squadron: with a loan from a friendly banker he bought an estate next to his own in Pomerania for 4 million marks and paid the debt that autumn with the sale of less than half the crop of one potato field; he bought 100 tons of maize for 8 million marks and sold it back a week later for double; early in 1923 he and six friends could not spend one dollar bill in a night in Berlin; his girlfriend's room cost half a pound of butter a month in 1922 and a whole pound by summer 1923. (b) Erna von Pustau's hosts in the country said candidly that they were paying off their mortgages; Fergusson adds that by August 1922 a mortgage seven or eight years old was 399/400ths paid off; her mother sold rented houses for twice the price paid and found furniture had risen fivefold. (c) Curt Riess: Stinnes signed contracts for millions and paid weeks later; his own father, a tailor, took only dollars. (d) Ullrich: owners of real assets and everyone who had debts and could now pay them off with worthless money were clearly privileged. Zweig's 'hundred dollars / £20 for rows of houses' is rhetoric, not a recorded sale. No named person who bought Berlin property with foreign currency was found.
fragments: Herr Hans-Georg von der Osten, who had formerly flown with Baron von Richthofen's Flying Circus
with a loan from a friendly banker, he bought an estate neighbouring his own property in Pomerania for 4 million marks
He paid the debt in the autumn with the sale of less than half the crop of one of his potato fields.
he bought 100 tons of maize from a dealer for 8 million marks (then about £5,000).
A week later, before it was even delivered, he sold the whole load back to the same dealer for double the amount
Finding himself with a single dollar bill early in 1923, von der Osten got hold of six friends
but early the next morning, long after dinner, and many nightclubs later, they still had change in their pockets.
half a pound of butter a month: by the summer of 1923 it was costing him a whole pound.
They replied candidly that they were paying off their mortgages.
He drew up a contract for so and so many millions only to pay these millions a few weeks later
From that day forward he made suits only for payment in dollars.
sowie alle, die Schulden gemacht hatten und diese nun mit wertlosem Geld abtragen konnten.
date_of_event: 1922 (estate, maize: Fergusson ch. 8; the reader gave June 1922 for the maize); early 1923 (dollar night); summer 1923 (butter rent)
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, chs. 5, 8, 9 (von der Osten's and von Pustau's recollections); Curt Riess (1990) on GHDI; Ullrich, APuZ 4/2023
note: Several von der Osten sentences came back whole (over the usual length): re-check wording before quoting. Fergusson does not say how he got von der Osten's story (apparently an interview). Later revaluation (Fergusson's narration): mortgages revalued at 15 per cent by the ordinance of 14 Feb 1924, raised to 25 per cent in July 1925; so 'the debt vanished' needs the qualifier that a fraction was restored later.

account: Other 1. Dorothea Günther (born 1914, Berlin; written June 2010 for LeMO): father paid daily, shop shutters down at noon
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (the museum's own eyewitness page; a childhood memory written 87 years later)
what_it_says: A shop she knew as a child (whose shop is not clear from the fragments read): in autumn 1923 the takings were milliards a day, then Billionen; old hundred and thousand notes were overprinted in red as million and milliard notes; the money was bundled and taken to the bank in big bags. Her father, a vocational-school teacher, was paid daily; when he came home at midday with a briefcase full of notes her mother ran to the grocer, and often came back disappointed because he had let the shutters down in front of her nose for the midday break, which he used to change the price tags. A woman called Berta (her role is not clear from the fragments) ran crying with her notes to her brother's shop, and he sold her one salt herring for the money.
fragments: Im Herbst 1923 wurden täglich Milliarden eingenommen, dann sogar Billionen.
Das Geld wurde nach dem Zählen gebündelt und in großen Taschen zur Bank gebracht.
Mein Vater, Gewerbeoberlehrer von Beruf, erhielt in dieser Zeit seine Gehaltszahlung täglich.
Wenn er mittags mit einer Aktentasche voller Geldscheine nach Hause kam, lief Mutter sofort zum Kaufmann.
Oft kam sie enttäuscht wieder, weil der Ladenbesitzer vor ihrer Nase die Rollläden heruntergelassen hatte: Mittagspause!
Die nutzte er dann, um die Preisschilder zu ändern.
Weinend rannte Berta mit den Geldscheinen hinunter in den Laden zu ihrem Bruder Wilhelm.
Und der verkaufte ihr für das Geld einen Salzhering.
source_name: LeMO Zeitzeugen (Deutsches Historisches Museum / Haus der Geschichte)
note: She was nine in 1923; written 87 years later. Whose shop it was and who Berta was did not come back from the reader: open the page before using those two details.

account: Other 2. Curt Riess (b. 1902), retrospective account 1990: wages weekly, then every three days, then daily; waiting for the dollar rate
verdict: FAITHFUL EXCERPT (GHDI translation)
what_it_says: Within a day a mark was worth half; it became the rule to pay workers and clerks weekly, then every three days, finally every day; with management's permission they rushed to the nearby shops; his father told him to wait each day for the announcement of the new dollar rate; his father the tailor took only dollars from then on.
fragments: Within one day, a mark was worth only half as much as the day before,
it became the rule to pay white and blue collar workers not monthly but weekly, then every three days and finally every day.
Then, with the permission of management, they rushed to the nearby shops and bought what they could.
He had admonished me to wait each day for the announcement of the new dollar exchange rate.
From that day forward he made suits only for payment in dollars.
Those who had lost everything were the great majority, however.
source_name: GHDI, from Riess in Pörtner (ed.), Alltag in der Weimarer Republik (ECON, 1990), pp. 33-36
note: Written 67 years later; the second fragment came back slightly over the usual length.

account: Other 3. Berlin's daily price list in the press, August 1923 (Fergusson)
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Fergusson quoting 'the press'; no newspaper named)
what_it_says: Each morning the papers printed the day's prices and multipliers: tram fare 50,000; monthly tram season ticket for one line 4 million, all lines 12 million; taxis multiply the ordinary fare by 600,000; horse cabs by 1,400,000; bookshops by 300,000; public baths by 115,000; medical attendance by 80,000.
fragments: In the press each morning would be published a list of the day's prices:
Tramway fare 50,000
Tramway monthly season ticket for one line 4 million
for all lines 12 million
Taxi-autos: multiply ordinary fare by 600,000
Horse cabs: multiply ordinary fare by 1,400,000
Bookshops: multiply ordinary price by 300,000
Public baths: multiply ordinary price by 115,000
Medical attendance: multiply ordinary price by 80,000
date_of_event: August 1923, Berlin (Fergusson's placement; no day given)
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, ch. 10
note: Useful beside Haffner's season ticket: a one-line monthly tram ticket at 4 million in August 1923. Unsourced beyond 'the press'.

account: Other 4. Joseph Addison, British embassy counsellor, private letter of 11 September 1923, and the Bavarian peasant
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Fergusson quoting Foreign Office papers)
what_it_says: Shops demand pounds, francs, Danish crowns; a housewife may stand from 8 am to 1 pm for a piece of sausage she does not get; a Bavarian peasant refused to sell him an egg for paper marks, calling Reichsbank notes 'Jew-scraps from Berlin'.
fragments: The shops are demanding pounds, francs, Danish crowns and any other foreign currency you may care to enumerate.
stand from 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. for a piece of sausage which in the end she does not get.
Judenfetzen von Berlin
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, ch. 11
note: The peasant's phrase is antisemitic; if used, it needs framing.

account: Other 5. George Grosz: carrying money in a knapsack
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (quoted by Facing History with page reference)
what_it_says: Lingering at a shop window was a luxury because shopping had to be done at once; people carted their money in wagons and knapsacks; he used a knapsack.
fragments: Lingering at the [shop] window was a luxury because shopping had to be done immediately.
People had to start carting their money around in wagons and knapsacks.
I used a knapsack.
source_name: Facing History, citing Grosz, A Little Yes and a Big No (Dial, 1946), p. 63

account: Other 6. British consul-general Robert Clive, Munich, 18 October 1923
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Fergusson quoting consular reports)
what_it_says: Few families can afford meat more than once a week, eggs are unprocurable, milk terribly scarce, and bread is sixteen times the price of a few days ago, when the maximum price was abolished.
fragments: The distress is very great.
Few families can afford meat more than once a week, eggs are unprocurable, milk terribly scarce
and bread already sixteen times the price of a few days ago when the maximum price was abolished.
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, ch. 12
note: Munich, not Berlin.

account: Other 7. Erna von Pustau and the street phrase for the falling mark
verdict: RETELLING ONLY (Fergusson quoting Buck)
what_it_says: People said 'the dollar is going up again' although the dollar was stable and the mark was falling: the root of 'the dollar' as daily talk, which Haffner and Kollwitz (the child on the tram asking 'is that the dollar?') confirm independently.
fragments: We used to say 'The dollar is going up again', while in reality the dollar remained stable but our mark was falling.
source_name: Fergusson, When Money Dies, ch. 1

account: Other 8. 'Havensteinrubel': the street name for the August 1923 million notes
verdict: ORIGINAL (a 1923 journal article)
what_it_says: Kurt Singer wrote in 1923 that the man in the street called the coloured million notes of the August 1923 type 'Havenstein roubles'.
fragments: Als der Mann der Straße die bunten Millionenscheine (Typung August 1923) mit dem Namen Havensteinrubel belegte
source_name: Kurt Singer, 'Der Fall Havenstein', Wirtschaftsdienst 8 (1923), Heft 33, pp. 797-798
